steps.narration: You are here because countless causes lined up to bring you to this screen. This path shows them as one continuous chain, from the first moment of the universe to this exact moment of your attention. Cause only runs one way: every link makes the next one possible, and nothing rewinds. As you follow it, notice what endures and what fades, and how much had to cooperate for you to exist. We will keep returning to that idea as time, space, life, and history converge on you.

To fit thirteen point eight billion years into something you can see, time circles a stretched, super logarithmic clock: the Big Bang sits at six oâclock, life begins near ten. At three oâclock, about five thousand years ago, the circle breaks into a straight road. That road is human history, moving one steady step per year toward now. The scale keeps changing because scales must change; a billion years and a single human lifetime both matter here, and you will watch the graph bend to make each readable.

Everything you see fits into three stacked layers. Red is matter: stars, planets, rocks, oceans, air. Green is life: cells, lineages, ecosystems. Blue is humans: cultures, economies, families, you. The stack matters because each level rises from the level beneath it. No life without matterâs chemistry. No humans without lifeâs long inheritance. When the camera drifts upward into green or blue, remember the red foundation still runs underneath, holding the whole structure in place. That dependency is part of the one way arrow of cause and effect.

The path hugs an inner track that marks your own lineage. Staying close means closer to you: our universe, our galaxy, our Sun, our Earth, the first cells that became animals, then apes, then people, then civilizations. Each thing that split away from our line glides outward and fades with distance. Other galaxies, other planets, other species, other peoples all mattered, but to your particular story they matter a little less. This is not about importance in the universe. It is about causal relevance to you.

No single zoom level can show both star birth and your birthday, so the graph reshapes itself. Focus on any era and that segment unrolls into its own timeline. Now a billion years can fill the screen, or one human life can. You are watching a constantly changing map of scale: deep time on a circle, recent time on a road, and any stretch straightened when needed. The tour will do this for you. Later, press U or the number keys to reshape the path yourself.

At the Big Bang, all space, matter, and energy began expanding from an unimaginably hot, dense state. In a fleeting instant, inflation likely stretched tiny quantum ripples into the patterns that seeded every later galaxy. That is the first red link beneath your feet. The hydrogen in your body took form as the universe cooled. The arrow of cause starts here and never points back. Everything afterward depends on this expanding stage, and that is why the red layer runs under every living thing and every human story.

As temperatures fell, quarks bound into protons and neutrons. Matter and antimatter then met and almost erased each other, but a tiny imbalance left about one extra matter particle in a billion. In the first minutes, some of that matter fused into helium. The result was a universe of about seventy five percent hydrogen and twenty five percent helium by mass, the fuel and raw material for all future stars. A hairâs breadth in the early balance made a universe where chemistry, planets, and you could exist.

About three hundred eighty thousand years in, the universe cooled enough for electrons to join protons and helium nuclei. Atoms formed, and light, no longer trapped by charged particles, streamed freely. We still see that glow today as the cosmic microwave background. Then the lights dimmed. For roughly a hundred million years, no stars burned. Gravity worked quietly, gathering dark matter and gas into denser knots. The scene looks still, but the next causes are assembling, slow and inevitable, preparing the conditions for the first stars.

Gravityâs knots tightened until the first stars ignited. Born from only hydrogen and helium, many were probably giants that lived fast and died young. In their cores, fusion forged heavier elements; in their explosions, they scattered carbon, oxygen, and iron into space. These were the ingredients of rocks, water, and lifeâs chemistry. Each stellar generation was both an effect of earlier clumps and a cause of richer matter later. The red layer learns to build complexity here, step by step, until worlds with oceans become possible.

Stars gathered into the first galaxies, and the red layer branched. Most ordinary matter stayed as a thin intergalactic gas. Many galaxies drifted outward, away from our track, while some merged, grew, and spun new stars. As space keeps expanding, and faster since dark energy took over, matter spreads thinner between islands of light. Our path follows one such island, and others fade with distance. What looks like drift here is the widening reach of cause: many possible futures, most of them not ours.

Our island is the Milky Way. Beginning about thirteen point six billion years ago, it grew by swallowing smaller galaxies and by turning gas into stars. Each generation died and enriched the remaining gas with heavier elements. Over billions of years that metallicity rose until carbon for organics and iron for cores were common. When you look at the Milky Way on this map, you are seeing the factory that prepared the Sun, the Earth, and eventually you. A galaxyâs patient cycles set your stage.

About four point six billion years ago, a cold cloud in the Milky Wayâs disk collapsed under gravity. That cloud was not pristine; it held dust and heavy elements made by earlier stars. Most material fell inward and heated to become the newborn Sun. The rest flattened into a spinning disk, where dust stuck to dust, growing pebbles, then boulders, then planetesimals. You are watching a new sub plot branch from the red layer, where leftover star stuff begins arranging itself into places life could land.

The Sun ignited and has shone steadily for more than four and a half billion years, holding roughly ninety nine point eight six percent of the solar systemâs mass. Almost every leaf, breath, and heartbeat on Earth is powered by sunlight. In the surrounding disk, the leftovers built Jupiter and the other planets, each veering off here onto its own outer track. Our story stays on the inner line, not because the others are unimportant, but because the next link for you is Earth.

About four point five four billion years ago, colliding planetesimals built the Earth at just the right distance from the Sun for liquid water. Heat from impacts and radioactivity melted it, and heavy iron sank to form a core while rock rose to make a mantle and crust. Later, the churning core would power a magnetic field that shields the air and oceans from the solar wind. The red layer is now a planetary engine, setting up the conditions the green layer will need.

Soon after Earth formed, a Mars sized body, often called Theia, likely struck it. The debris ringed the Earth and coalesced into the Moon. That new companion steadied Earthâs tilt, keeping seasons and climate more stable over deep time. The Moon also raised strong tides that sculpted coastlines and stirred shallow seas where early life found changing, nutrient rich environments. A single violent accident became a stabilizing presence. Cause and effect can be fierce in the short term and gentle in the long.

By about four point four billion years ago, Earth likely had liquid water. Near ten oâclock on the deep time clock, faint carbon traces in ancient Greenland rocks suggest microbes lived by three point seven billion years ago. Here the green layer begins. Every living thing on Earth, from bacteria to trees to you, descends from one common ancestor. We still carry its genetic code. Matter has now arranged itself into something that copies, varies, and persists. From this, all later life unfolds.

From that first ancestor, the tree of life spreads into the green layer you see here. Our own lineage tracks the inner edge; every branch that split away bends outward and fades with distance. The living tips are grouped into about one thousand six hundred families. Within each branch, predator and prey are ordered by the food chain, with top hunters toward the inside. This is a map of kinship and energy flow together, showing who came from whom, and who eats whom, across time.

Early microbes drew energy from chemistry or from sunlight without making oxygen. By about three billion years ago, cyanobacteria learned to split water using light. That trick harvested energy from an almost universal resource and poured it into life. The waste product, oxygen, began to leak into the oceans and air. Here you can feel the green layer gaining global influence. Once life learned to use water and light, the sunlight striking Earth each day became fuel for evolutionâs long experiments, including the one that leads to you.

About two point four billion years ago, oxygen finally built up in the atmosphere. For many microbes it was a poison, and the change likely helped trigger a long ice age. But oxygen also formed an ozone shield against ultraviolet light and made high energy breathing possible. Life had changed the chemistry of the planet, and the planetâs new chemistry changed life in return. This is how causes stack: red shapes green, green reshapes red, and both prepare the ground for the blue layer to come.

With oxygen available, breathing became a powerful way to extract energy. By about one point six five billion years ago, an archaeon likely took in an oxygen breathing bacterium that became the mitochondrion. That partnership turned meals into more usable energy and let cells grow larger and more complex. From these eukaryotes would come plants, fungi, and animals. Brains are expensive, and this is the step that could pay their costs. The green layer has invented internal cooperation, and complexity begins to climb.

Once cells could afford the energy, they began to specialize and cooperate as bodies. The red alga Bangiomorpha, about a billion years old, shows the first known sexual reproduction, mixing genes to speed evolution. Complex cells branched into green plants, fungi, and animals. Fungi are closer kin to us than to plants, a reminder that appearance can mislead while ancestry clarifies. Multicellularity is a new way to solve problems: billions of tiny units acting as one, a pattern the blue layer will echo.

After Snowball Earthâs deep freezes, thawing oceans flooded with nutrients. Soft bodied Ediacaran creatures appeared, and then, from about five hundred thirty nine million years ago, most animal body plans arose within some twenty million years. Eyes saw. Shells shielded. Predators and prey pushed each other into faster, sharper designs. This Cambrian explosion set the main cast of animal forms. Our own branch, with backbones and brains, will take that toolkit onto land, but the rules of the arms race were written here.

In the Cambrian seas, our line shows up as chordates, small swimmers with a flexible rod along the back. Over time, skulls grew to protect larger brains, vertebrae replaced the rod, and hinged jaws let early fish become active predators. That blueprint for sensing, moving, and deciding is the one you still use. The green layer now builds on its own inventions: nerves, muscles, and bones feedback into better behavior, and behavior into survival. The chain continues, cause atop cause, toward land.

Around four hundred seventy million years ago, plants crept onto land. They held water, forged alliances with fungi, and slowly turned bare rock into soil. As they spread, they pulled carbon dioxide from the air, altered climate, and within about eighty five million years raised the first forests. The continents changed character. Rivers, soils, and shade created new niches. Plant life made land livable for animals, just as earlier microbes had prepared the air and seas. The stage for backboned walkers was set.

Following the greenery, lobe finned fish with sturdy internal bones explored shallows and swamps. About three hundred seventy million years ago, their fins reshaped into limbs, and tetrapods stepped onto land. Those bones became your arm and leg bones. They survived the Late Devonian extinction and diversified. A vertebrate body that mastered buoyancy now learned to bear weight, breathe air, and hear in a new medium. The green layer keeps translating old solutions into new environments, and our particular path stays on the inner track.

Amphibians still had to return to water to breed. Amniotes solved that constraint with eggs that carry their own water and protective membranes. Freed from ponds, they spread across dry land. Their line split in two great branches. One side led to reptiles and birds. The other, our inner track, led to mammals. From here, the story narrows toward warm blood, hair, and parental care. A new pattern appears: investing energy in fewer, better protected young, a costly bet that will pay off later.

About two hundred fifty two million years ago, immense eruptions in Siberia heated and acidified the planet. The Great Dying erased over eighty percent of marine species and devastated life on land. Here you can feel red resetting green. Extinctions remove options, but they also open niches. In the battered, recovering world, the dinosaur line grew dominant, and the mammal line, our own, persisted in small shadows. Cause is not kind or cruel; it is indifferent. What survives becomes the next starting point.

Dinosaurs arose about two hundred thirty three million years ago and, after the end Triassic extinction, ruled the land for roughly one hundred thirty five million years. Under their feet, the first mammals endured as small, mostly nocturnal insect eaters. Warm blood kept them active in the dark. Fur and keen hearing helped them survive. Across this long span, the green layer refined both lines. Dominance is not destiny; it is a chapter. Our chapter waits for a sudden red event to turn the page.

Sixty six million years ago, an asteroid about ten kilometers wide slammed into what is now Mexicoâs Yucatan. Dust and aerosols darkened the sky, cooling the planet and collapsing food webs. About three quarters of species died, including all non bird dinosaurs. Watch red strike green and redraw possibilities. Without this single impact, mammals might never have escaped the shadows, and we might not be here. Catastrophe and opportunity can be the same event, depending on which branches survive to tell the story.

With dinosaurs gone, placental mammals radiated into the empty niches. Whales returned to the sea. Bats took the night sky. Horses, cats, and dogs claimed the plains and forests. Primates, our branch, explored the trees. Within each branch the food chain orders the groups: hunters such as cats sit toward the inside, the plant eaters they rely on lie a little farther out. The green layer is now a web of interlocking causes, where what one group eats helps build what the next group can do.

One small line climbed into the canopy. Primates evolved grasping hands, forward facing eyes, and, in many species, keen color vision useful for fruit and leaves. They formed complex social groups that rewarded memory and negotiation. Apes stretched this further, with bigger brains, longer childhoods for learning, and rich relationships. The green layer is starting to support the kind of minds that can carry culture. The path to you runs through these branches, from balancing on branches to thinking about thinking.

As African climates cooled and forests opened into woodlands and grasslands, our lineage split from the chimpanzeesâ by about seven million years ago. Walking upright freed the hands for carrying and, eventually, for making and using tools. Bipedalism also changed how we kept cool and how far we could travel. Step by step, a new way of being an ape took shape. Notice how many causes are environmental and anatomical long before they are cultural. The blue layer is still below the horizon, waiting.

Free hands began to shape stone. The oldest known tools are about three point three million years old. Sharper edges opened bones and bodies for meat and marrow, feeding larger, more energy hungry brains. Later, Homo erectus spread beyond Africa. Mastery of fire and cooking released even more energy from food and softened timeâs pressures by extending daylight and warmth. Swinging ice age climates rewarded adaptability over specialization. Culture begins as a survival tool here, setting up the leap the blue layer will make.

About three hundred thousand years ago, our own species appears in Africa. Language and shared culture let knowledge accumulate faster than genes can change, turning learning itself into an engine of evolution. That is why a third, blue layer rises above lifeâs green. In blue, ideas inherit from ideas. The arrow of cause adds a new track, built on the same red matter and green biology but moving on its own rules. From here, the chain will tighten around tools, symbols, and stories.

Carrying tools, fire, and culture, modern humans spread from Africa into Asia, Europe, and Australia, and later into the Americas, starting around seventy thousand years ago. Along the way they met and mixed with Neanderthals and Denisovans, who later vanished as distinct groups. Every culture outside Africa descends from these waves of migration. On this path, the blue layer expands across the map while the green and red layers provide the ground and the food. Movement reshaped who could meet whom, and what they could share.

When the last ice age ended eleven thousand seven hundred years ago, the Holoceneâs stable climate made farming possible. People domesticated grasses like wheat and rice, whose large seeds store food, and began herding animals. Surpluses freed some hands from constant foraging, leading to villages, cities, writing, and the first civilizations. In blue, population and complexity rise together. In green and red, the focus shifts from wild webs to managed fields and herds. The next links will show humans arranging the layers beneath them.

Farming pulled certain wild families into service. Wheat, sheep, goats, and cattle left the green tree of life about ten thousand five hundred years ago and climbed into a new stratum just under people: livestock and crops. There, their lifelines run parallel to ours. Today, livestock outweighs all wild mammals by more than ten to one. The blue layer now directly steers part of the green. That control is a cause with many effects, from diet and disease to landscapes and languages.

Beneath the farms lies the matter we extract. Early copper smelting, then bronze and iron, drew metal out of Earthâs red layer and into tools, weapons, and trade. Coal, oil, and finally concrete turned a human trickle into a torrent, roughly one hundred billion tonnes a year. On this map, humans sit on top, the life we manage just below, and the minerals, fuels, and sand we dig below that. Blue reshapes green and red together, and those changes flow back into blue.

Civilizations appear in blue as flowing streams. Their widths represent relative power, taken from John Sparksâs nineteen thirty one Histomap and, for the last century, from shares of world GDP. When the Histomap begins, around two thousand BCE, Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Anatolian, Indian, and Chinese peoples already flow side by side. Streams merge, split, and swell. You can see how influence is never single threaded. Many causes act at once, and power is a moving average of food, metals, ideas, and luck.

Look inside any stream and you will find people. Each stream contains a population curve split by sex, men on one side and women on the other. Every thin line is a lifespan, its height rising and falling with a modeled social market value. Each line stands in for many people; the number is shown on screen. Famous figures glow, from Hatshepsut to Hammurabi, but most lines are ordinary lives. History is built from all of them, and your line will sit here too.

Why do so many lines stop short? In ancient times, life expectancy at birth was about twenty six years, mostly because many children died very young. Adults who reached fifteen often lived into their forties, fifties, or sixties. Compare the two halves as you move forward. Womenâs small edge in lifespan widened as childbirth became safer, to roughly five years today. On this graph, demographic causes become visible scars and bulges. The blue layerâs averages hide huge personal differences, yet every life is counted.

Streams collide and split. Egypt and the Hittites fought to a draw at Kadesh and signed one of the oldest known peace treaties. Yet around twelve hundred BCE, the Late Bronze Age collapse toppled the Hittites and the Aegean palaces. Trade routes broke. Palatial centers burned. Populations shrank. In time, from the wreckage grew the Greek city states. On this map, you can watch a thick stream break into thinner ones, and then see new currents gather strength from scattered sources.

As Iron Age states grew larger and richer, thinkers across Eurasia asked how to live well and what a just order might be. Confucius and Laozi in China, the Buddha in India, and Socrates in Greece offered answers that outlived every empire on this map. Ideas move differently from armies. They can leap across borders, hibernate in books, and return centuries later. The blue layer is now clearly about information as well as power, and those ideas still shape billions of people, including you.

Cyrus the Great built Persia into the largest empire yet. Alexander the Great conquered it in under a decade, carrying Greek soldiers and scholars from the Aegean to the Indus. When he died at thirty two, his empire split among his generals. Watch Greek rule flow into Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucid Empire. Greek language and learning spread with those currents, mixing with Egyptian, Persian, and Indian traditions. Conquest is a cause, but so is the mingling that follows it, long after flags change.

Rome absorbed Greek culture, destroyed Carthage in the Punic Wars, and, after Julius Caesarâs civil war, became an empire under Augustus. Roads, law, and Latin knit the Mediterranean into one economic and cultural basin. The eastern half, Byzantium, endured until fourteen fifty three and preserved much Greek learning. Here you can watch one stream grow wide by organizing flows of grain, silver, and ideas. Empires look solid on a map, but their strength is the tangle of connections they keep open.

The scriptures of little Israel and Judah shaped faiths that outlasted empires. Christianity spread along Romeâs roads after Jesus and Paul. Islam united Arabia under Muhammad and then under caliphates that stretched from Spain to India. Those states preserved Greek science and carried Indian numerals west. Religious ideas became networks that bound strangers into communities, polities, and trade routes. On this map, the brightest lines are not always the widest streams. Influence can flow through belief and learning as well as armies.

Steppe nomads such as the Huns pressed Germanic peoples into a weakened Roman West. By four seventy six, the Western Empire had fallen. Watch one wide stream split into many: the Franks, peaking under Charlemagne, and other Germanic kingdoms that became the roots of France, Germany, England, and more. The blue layer often forks rather than fades. Institutions fracture, but people, laws, and languages continue down narrower channels. What looks like collapse from a distance can be, up close, a redistribution of causes.

In the twelve hundreds, Genghis Khan and his heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Their conquests linked Eurasiaâs trade routes, moving goods, ideas, and, tragically, diseases like the Black Death. As the empire fractured, new powers rose at its edges, including Muscovy, later Russia, and the Ottoman Turks. On this map, a single surge triggers many secondary currents. The blue layer shows how connectivity amplifies both creativity and catastrophe, and how the end of one empire seeds the next.

Around fourteen fifty, Gutenbergâs press made books much cheaper. Printed ideas spread faster than any ruler could stop them, fueling Lutherâs Reformation and the new sciences of Galileo and Newton. Meanwhile, Columbusâs fourteen ninety two voyage linked Europe and the Americas, sending crops, metals, microbes, and people both ways. The printing press and the Columbian exchange multiplied feedback loops. Knowledge accelerated. Economies globalized. On this graph, you can watch streams widen not just through conquest, but by compressing space and time with information.

Printing, science, and trade fed two great revolutions in the late seventeen hundreds. Britainâs American colonies declared independence in seventeen seventy six, launching a political experiment in self government. At the same time, James Wattâs improved steam engines helped ignite Britainâs Industrial Revolution. Machines amplified each workerâs output, factories reorganized labor, and energy from coal replaced muscle and wind. The British, then American, streams swelled with power. Blue now begins to run on fossil sunlight stored in red rock.

Industry funded science, and science lengthened lives. Germ theory, vaccines, antibiotics, clean water, and high yield crops slashed child mortality and more than doubled global life expectancy since eighteen hundred, to over seventy years today. On this map, lifelines stretch out, and population curves billow. The green and red layers bend under the weight of more people living longer. This is cause and effect made visible: knowledge and energy change survival, which changes everything from cities to carbon to your grandparentsâ chances to meet.

The same industry that raised living standards also made war industrial. World War One killed about twenty million people, and World War Two about seventy five million. In this model, roughly a quarter of German and a fifth of Soviet military age men die, a scar you can see as a gap on the menâs side of those streams. The blue layer concentrates both power and risk. When mass production turns to destruction, the losses reshape families, economies, and the next generationâs possibilities.

By nineteen forty five, the United States was by far the widest stream, now measured by share of world GDP. In the decades after, Japan and Germany rebuilt into economic giants. Since Deng Xiaopingâs reforms began in nineteen seventy eight, China has grown into the largest economy by purchasing power, and India is rising fast. Power keeps flowing, splitting, and merging. On this graph, you can see that no stream stays widest forever. The map adapts, just as your view must, to shifting scales.

For most of history, the human branch was a thin thread. After eighteen hundred, coal, medicine, and fertilizer let population leap from about one billion to more than eight billion. Every layer beneath blue exploded with it: livestock herds, cropland, fuels, ores, and sand. This acceleration is not one cause, but a tangle. Energy unlocked industry, industry funded science, science lengthened lives, and more people demanded more energy and matter. The rates you see here are the background conditions of your own life.

Inside civilizations, famous lines glow so you can follow them, and threads connect who shaped whom: Newton to Einstein, teacher to student, mentor to critic. Press F at any moment to see the people alive right then, and trace any of them from birth to death. The blue layer is networks atop networks. Ideas propagate through friendships, rivalries, and institutions. Your own path is also a mesh of influences. Even watching this tour adds a thread, linking you to what and whom you learn from.

Letâs zoom into one stream, the United States from nineteen fifty to today. Here, the population is simulated in detail from United Nations age pyramids and from US marriage and divorce rates. Men are on one side, women on the other. The reason to zoom is scale. A nation over seventy years can fill the screen so that individual lifelines become visible. Inside the wide blue current, you can now watch births, pairings, separations, and deaths as they actually stack up through time.

Each line follows one life from birth to death. From age eighteen, its height follows a modeled social market value. In this model, womenâs value peaks younger on average, menâs rises with wealth into middle age, and having children lowers both by shifting time and attention. It is a drawn version of a popular idea, made visible so you can examine it, not a measurement of peopleâs worth. Models are tools. Use them to ask better questions, and to notice what they leave out.

No screen could draw hundreds of millions of Americans one by one, so each line stands for many people. Watch the count on screen change as you zoom, because scale is part of the story. Higher value lines run nearest the center line between the two halves. Married couples are drawn inward, side by side, reflecting shared status and resources. When a pair splits, their lines drift apart. By compressing time and stacking lives, you can see patterns in the blue layer that everyday life hides.

When World War Two ended, returning soldiers, early marriages, and rising prosperity produced the baby boom. US births surged from nineteen forty six to nineteen sixty four. On this zoomed view, childrenâs lines sprout from their parentsâ lines. You can watch the boomers branch from the Greatest and Silent generations like a sudden thicket. That bulge then moves forward through school, work, and retirement. Demography is slow motion destiny in blue, a cause that keeps shaping politics, housing, and family life for decades.

From nineteen sixty to nineteen eighty, the US divorce rate more than doubled, and later the marriage rate fell by over a third. On this map, more paired lines come apart, often after children have branched from them. Millennials, Gen Z, and Generation Alpha inherit later marriages, more cohabitation, and fewer children on average. Causes shift from institutions to choices, and from norms to economics. The blue layer is flexible, but not free; culture, policy, and prices still steer where those lines tend to go.

The human branch runs straight to its tip. The last century is a thin slice of it. The last year is a hairline. The last second is invisible. Yet every blue line is still arriving here, one life at a time. Far behind, green and red faded into the background before blue began, but what they made possible continues in us. This is the arrow of cause made plain: nothing runs backward, everything accumulates, and the path keeps narrowing into the present you occupy.

At the glowing Now beacon, all three layers arrive together. Your hydrogen dates from the Big Bang. Your carbon and oxygen were cooked in stars. Three point seven billion years of life honed the cells that build your body and brain. Every empire, war, discovery, harvest, and family in blue shaped your language, tools, and options. On this graph, every line either ended along the way or led here, to you. This is the only place you can act, and the only time.

Now step back. From the Big Bang at six oâclock, around the clock of deep time, and down the human branch, everything before led to this moment. This moment is also where the next chain of causes begins. Explore any era, follow lines from cause to effect, and watch scales bend to fit what you need to see. However far you roam on the map, it always returns to one point: you, here, now, watching, deciding what to do with what made you possible.
